claim: Macrophages are key immune cells with important roles for tissue surveillance in almost all mammalian organs.
source: Macrophages are key immune cells with important roles for tissue surveillance in almost all mammalian organs.
evidence: This is a general statement about macrophage function that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Surveying macrophage populations can tolerate lowered actomyosin contractility.
source: We show that surveying macrophage populations can tolerate lowered actomyosin contractility, but cannot easily compensate for a lack of integrin-mediated adhesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Y27632 treatment (which lowers actomyosin contractility) does not impair the sampling efficiency of macrophage populations.

claim: Surveying macrophage populations cannot easily compensate for a lack of integrin-mediated adhesion.
source: We show that surveying macrophage populations can tolerate lowered actomyosin contractility, but cannot easily compensate for a lack of integrin-mediated adhesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs showed impaired bead internalization and efferocytosis in 3D matrices.

claim: Integrins were dispensable for macrophage chemotactic responses.
source: Although integrins were dispensable for macrophage chemotactic responses, they were crucial to control cell movement and protrusiveness for optimal surveillance by a macrophage population.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs moved at comparable speeds to WT cells along C5a gradients.

claim: Integrins were crucial to control cell movement and protrusiveness for optimal surveillance by a macrophage population.
source: Although integrins were dispensable for macrophage chemotactic responses, they were crucial to control cell movement and protrusiveness for optimal surveillance by a macrophage population.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that integrin-deficient macrophages had impaired random motility and reduced bead/dead cell clearance.

claim: β1 integrins are important for maintaining macrophage shape and network sampling efficiency in mammalian tissues.
source: Our study reveals that β1 integrins are important for maintaining macrophage shape and network sampling efficiency in mammalian tissues, and sets macrophage motility strategies apart from the integrin-independent 3D migration modes of many other immune cell subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both in vitro and in vivo experiments showing morphological changes and functional deficits in β1 integrin-deficient macrophages.

claim: Macrophage motility strategies are set apart from the integrin-independent 3D migration modes of many other immune cell subsets.
source: Our study reveals that β1 integrins are important for maintaining macrophage shape and network sampling efficiency in mammalian tissues, and sets macrophage motility strategies apart from the integrin-independent 3D migration modes of many other immune cell subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous studies on other immune cells and the experimental data showing integrin-dependence of macrophage random motility.

claim: Macrophages distribute in numerous mammalian tissues to form large networks of many individual cells.
source: It is well established that macrophages distribute in numerous mammalian tissues to form large networks of many individual cells (Dawson et al., 2020; Freitas-Lopes et al., 2017; Gordon et al., 2014; Honda et al., 2020; Jain and Weninger, 2013; Nicolás-Ávila et al., 2020; Stolp et al., 2020; Uderhardt et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The population aspect of macrophage efferocytosis in tissues has so far only received little attention.
source: However, the population aspect of macrophage efferocytosis in tissues has so far only received little attention and the single-cell parameters that critically determine the efferocytic capacity of a whole macrophage population are only poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: The single-cell parameters that critically determine the efferocytic capacity of a whole macrophage population are only poorly understood.
source: However, the population aspect of macrophage efferocytosis in tissues has so far only received little attention and the single-cell parameters that critically determine the efferocytic capacity of a whole macrophage population are only poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field that motivates the current study.

claim: Leukocyte migration in three-dimensional (3D) interstitial spaces is considered flexible and adaptive.
source: Leukocyte migration in three-dimensional (3D) interstitial spaces is considered flexible and adaptive, with many immune cells switching to alternate migration modes upon perturbations of any of these three components (Lämmermann and Sixt, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Many immune cells switch to alternate migration modes upon perturbations of actin polymerization, actomyosin contraction, or adhesion.
source: Leukocyte migration in three-dimensional (3D) interstitial spaces is considered flexible and adaptive, with many immune cells switching to alternate migration modes upon perturbations of any of these three components (Lämmermann and Sixt, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Leukocyte motility outside the vasculature relies almost exclusively on cell shape changes driven by the actomyosin cytoskeleton.
source: Previous work on these cell types has highlighted that leukocyte motility outside the vasculature relies almost exclusively on cell shape changes driven by the actomyosin cytoskeleton (Lämmermann et al., 2013; Lämmermann et al., 2008; Woolf et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Amoeboid migration is independent from integrin adhesion receptors and strong adhesive interactions with the tissue environment.
source: This migration mode, commonly referred to as amoeboid migration, is independent from integrin adhesion receptors and strong adhesive interactions with the tissue environment (Paluch et al., 2016; Reversat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Macrophages in zebrafish larvae move with elongated morphology at lower speeds and show adhesion structures containing heterodimeric integrin receptors.
source: Macrophages in zebrafish larvae (Barros-Becker et al., 2017) and human monocyte-derived macrophages (hMDMs) invading into 3D matrigels (Van Goethem et al., 2011; Van Goethem et al., 2010) move with elongated morphology at lower speeds and show adhesion structures containing heterodimeric integrin receptors (Hynes, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human monocyte-derived macrophages invading into 3D matrigels move with elongated morphology at lower speeds and show adhesion structures containing heterodimeric integrin receptors.
source: Macrophages in zebrafish larvae (Barros-Becker et al., 2017) and human monocyte-derived macrophages (hMDMs) invading into 3D matrigels (Van Goethem et al., 2011; Van Goethem et al., 2010) move with elongated morphology at lower speeds and show adhesion structures containing heterodimeric integrin receptors (Hynes, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Macrophages in mice protrude elongated processes for tissue surveillance in almost all organs.
source: Macrophages in mice also protrude elongated processes for tissue surveillance in almost all organs.
evidence: This is a general statement about macrophage morphology in mice that is supported by the authors' observations and established knowledge.

claim: Macrophages are well known as very adhesive cell type with a broad range of different integrin adhesion receptors on their surface.
source: Moreover, they are well known as very adhesive cell type with a broad range of different integrin adhesion receptors on their surface (Ley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Hemocytes move in highly confined, fluid-filled spaces, where only over time these macrophages together with other cells deposit extracellular matrix (ECM).
source: Hemocytes move in highly confined, fluid-filled spaces, where only over time these macrophages together with other cells deposit extracellular matrix (ECM) (Matsubayashi et al., 2017; Sánchez-Sánchez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Individual BMDMs moved with mesenchymal-like elongated shapes at average speeds of ~0.6 µm/min in 3D matrigel.
source: By combining this system with video-based brightfield microscopy, we monitored migration dynamics in macrophage populations over 24–30 hr and found that individual cells moved with mesenchymal-like elongated shapes at average speeds of ~0.6 µm/min (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Treatment of BMDMs with cytochalasin D revealed an essential requirement of actin dynamics for macrophage random migration.
source: Treatment of BMDMs with the F-actin-disrupting drug cytochalasin D, the Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) inhibitor Y27632 or the non-muscle myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin revealed an essential requirement of actin dynamics and an important role of actomyosin contraction for macrophage random migration (Figure 1C–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of BMDMs with Y27632 or blebbistatin revealed an important role of actomyosin contraction for macrophage random migration.
source: Treatment of BMDMs with the F-actin-disrupting drug cytochalasin D, the Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) inhibitor Y27632 or the non-muscle myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin revealed an essential requirement of actin dynamics and an important role of actomyosin contraction for macrophage random migration (Figure 1C–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of BMDMs with CK-666 caused cell rounding and loss of prominent mesenchymal protrusions in the majority of macrophages.
source: Treatment of BMDMs with the Arp2/3 complex inhibitor CK-666 caused cell rounding and loss of prominent mesenchymal protrusions in the majority of macrophages (Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—video 2.

claim: CK-666 treatment resulted in a significant reduction in the average speed of BMDMs.
source: This resulted in a significant reduction in the average speed, supporting an important role of dendritic actin filament networks for 3D macrophage random migration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tln1−/− BMDMs showed roundish, amoeboid-like morphologies and severely impaired random migration.
source: Tln1−/− BMDMs, which are depleted of talin, a crucial interactor with integrin cytoplasmic domains for integrin activation (Calderwood and Ginsberg, 2003), showed roundish, amoeboid-like morphologies and severely impaired random migration (Figure 1F–I and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-I and Figure 1—video 2.

claim: Tln1−/− cells were missing the prominent branched protrusions that gave WT macrophages their mesenchymal-like cell shape.
source: Confocal fluorescence microscopy of Lifeact-GFP expressing BMDMs in 3D matrices clearly revealed that Tln1−/− cells were missing the prominent branched protrusions that gave WT macrophages their mesenchymal-like cell shape (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Itgb2−/− BMDMs lack β2 integrins on the cell surface, including the strongly expressed heterodimer αMβ2 (Mac-1).
source: Itgb2−/− BMDMs lack β2 integrins on the cell surface, including the strongly expressed heterodimer αMβ2 (Mac-1), a characteristic macrophage cell surface protein with promiscuous binding properties to more than 30 non-protein and protein molecules, including several ECM components (Yakubenko et al., 2002; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citation to previous work.

claim: ITGB2 deficiency did not result in cell shape changes or migration deficiencies.
source: Surprisingly, ITGB2 deficiency did not result in cell shape changes or migration deficiencies (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: Itgb1−/− BMDMs copied the morphology and migration phenotype of Tln1−/− BMDMs.
source: However, Itgb1−/− BMDMs that lack the important ECM-binding heterodimers α5β1 and α6β1 on their cell surface, copied the morphology and migration phenotype of Tln1−/− BMDMs (Figure 1F–I; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F-I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Loss of integrin functionality and the associated switch from mesenchymal-like to amoeboid morphology results in severely impaired 3D motility, which macrophages cannot compensate in contrast to many other immune cell types.
source: Thus, our results identify a crucial role of β1 integrins for the mesenchymal-like movement of macrophages, highlighting the substrate-dependent (haptokinetic) nature of 3D macrophage random migration. Loss of integrin functionality and the associated switch from mesenchymal-like to amoeboid morphology results in severely impaired 3D motility, which macrophages cannot compensate in contrast to many other immune cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous studies on other immune cells.

claim: ITGB1 depletion caused macrophages in the interstitial spaces of the skin dermis to adopt a roundish, amoeboid-like cell shape.
source: In agreement with our findings from 3D matrigels, ITGB1 depletion caused macrophages in the interstitial spaces of the skin dermis (Figure 2A), the splenic red pulp (Figure 2B), and in the sinusoidal spaces of the liver (Figure 2C) to adopt a roundish, amoeboid-like cell shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: ITGB1 depletion caused macrophages in the splenic red pulp to adopt a roundish, amoeboid-like cell shape.
source: In agreement with our findings from 3D matrigels, ITGB1 depletion caused macrophages in the interstitial spaces of the skin dermis (Figure 2A), the splenic red pulp (Figure 2B), and in the sinusoidal spaces of the liver (Figure 2C) to adopt a roundish, amoeboid-like cell shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: ITGB1 depletion caused macrophages in the sinusoidal spaces of the liver to adopt a roundish, amoeboid-like cell shape.
source: In agreement with our findings from 3D matrigels, ITGB1 depletion caused macrophages in the interstitial spaces of the skin dermis (Figure 2A), the splenic red pulp (Figure 2B), and in the sinusoidal spaces of the liver (Figure 2C) to adopt a roundish, amoeboid-like cell shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Macrophages in tissues of Itgb2−/− mice retained their mesenchymal-like morphologies.
source: In contrast, macrophages in tissues of Itgb2−/− mice retained their mesenchymal-like morphologies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of cytochalasin D and Y27632 treatment on chemotactic macrophage migration were comparable to the effects on random motility.
source: The effects of cytochalasin D and Y27632 treatment on chemotactic macrophage migration were comparable to our previous results on random motility (Figure 1C–E), showing an essential requirement for actin dynamics and an important role for actomyosin contraction (Figure 3B, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, D, and E.

claim: CK-666 treatment did not impair BMDM chemotaxis in 3D matrigel.
source: CK-666 treatment did not impair BMDM chemotaxis in 3D matrigel (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which is in agreement with previous studies showing that Arp2/3 complex blockade rather increases than decreases migration speed in several cell types (Asokan et al., 2014; Dimchev et al., 2021; Georgantzoglou et al., 2021; Leithner et al., 2016; Moreau et al., 2015; Rotty et al., 2017; Vargas et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs moved at comparable average speeds to WT and Itgb2−/− BMDMs along the C5a gradient.
source: Strikingly, the dependency on integrin function was markedly different between random and chemotactic macrophage migration. In contrast to random motility, Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs, which had adopted more roundish and amoeboid-like shapes, moved at comparable average speeds to WT and Itgb2−/− BMDMs, which migrated with very elongated and mesenchymal-like morphologies along the C5a gradient (Figure 3C, F and G and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, F, and G.

claim: Track straightness and cell surface expression of C5aR1 were comparable between all gene variants.
source: Track straightness and cell surface expression of C5aR1 were comparable between all gene variants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Y27632 treatment impaired the chemotactic migration of Tln1−/− BMDMs.
source: Y27632 treatment impaired the chemotactic migration of Tln1−/− BMDMs, supporting an important role of actomyosin contractility as amoeboid protrusive force for integrin-independent macrophage migration (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chemotactic guidance cues can overcome the migration deficit of adhesion-deficient macrophages and induce productive amoeboid-like, integrin-independent macrophage movement.
source: Thus, chemotactic guidance cues can overcome the migration deficit of adhesion-deficient macrophages and induce productive amoeboid-like, integrin-independent macrophage movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that integrin-deficient macrophages can migrate chemotactically.

claim: Most ITGB1-deficient macrophages lacked the typical multi-protrusive mesenchymal-like phenotype of WT macrophages in the unchallenged ear dermis.
source: In agreement with our immunofluorescence analysis of ear skin whole mount tissues (Figure 2A), 2P-IVM of GFP-positive macrophages in the unchallenged ear dermis confirmed that most ITGB1-deficient macrophages lacked the typical multi-protrusive mesenchymal-like phenotype of WT macrophages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: WT macrophages quickly formed long protrusions toward the tissue lesion, while most cell bodies remained immotile during the short observation period.
source: Imaging WT macrophages at high magnification revealed that these cells quickly formed long protrusions toward the tissue lesion, while most cell bodies remained immotile during this short observation period (Figure 4B and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: Itgb1−/− macrophages formed directed protrusions toward the damage site at comparable speeds to WT cells.
source: Although most Itgb1−/− macrophages displayed rounded morphologies in unchallenged skin, these cells also formed directed protrusions toward the damage site at comparable speeds to WT cells (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: A twofold increase in cell body displacement was observed for Itgb1−/− macrophages in comparison to WT macrophages during the wound response.
source: We observed for Itgb1−/− macrophages a twofold increase in cell body displacement (53% of all analyzed Itgb1−/− cells, N = 55) in comparison to WT macrophages (24% of all analyzed WT cells, N = 34), which we interpret as a switch to a more amoeboid migration mode (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A network of 400–500 macrophages was able to almost completely clear gels of a corresponding number of extracellular particles within 24 hr.
source: PS on the bead surface acted as an 'eat-me' signal for macrophages (Segawa and Nagata, 2015), and a network of 400–500 macrophages was able to almost completely clear gels of a corresponding number of extracellular particles within 24 hr (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cytochalasin D treatment inhibited macrophage space exploration and bead uptake over 24 hr.
source: Cytochalasin D treatment served as negative control for our analysis, as the complete stalling of migration and protrusion formation inhibited macrophage space exploration and bead uptake over 24 hr (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Lowering actomyosin contractility by Y27632 treatment did not impact the sampling efficiency of a macrophage population.
source: In contrast, lowering actomyosin contractility by Y27632 treatment did not impact the sampling efficiency of a macrophage population (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Y27632-treated macrophage populations showed equal space exploration and bead uptake as control populations despite individual BMDMs moving at only ~30% of their normal speed.
source: Although individual BMDMs moved under these conditions at only ~30% of their normal speed (Figure 1D–E), their gain in single-cell protrusiveness compensated for this reduction in speed and allowed Y27632-treated macrophage populations equal space exploration and bead uptake as control populations (Figure 5C and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Macrophage networks can use two equally efficient surveillance strategies: surveillance by migration and surveillance by low-motile protrusion extension.
source: Thus, macrophage networks can use two equally efficient surveillance strategies: (a) surveillance by migration (Figure 5G and Figure 3—video 1) and (b) surveillance by low-motile protrusion extension (Figure 5H and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Integrin-dependent deficits in macrophage random motility translated directly to impaired removal of extracellular particles in matrigel.
source: We then investigated how integrin-dependent haptokinesis influences the sampling efficiency of macrophage networks. We found that integrin-dependent deficits in macrophage random motility (Figure 1F–I) translated directly to impaired removal of extracellular particles in matrigel (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs had comparable phagocytic activity to WT controls when macrophages were kept as cell suspensions during the incubation with PS-attached beads.
source: Although Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs had comparable phagocytic activity to WT controls when macrophages were kept as cell suspensions during the incubation with PS-attached beads (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), these mutant BMDMs showed clearly reduced bead internalization in the 3D matrix (Figure 6B and C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs showed clearly reduced bead internalization in the 3D matrix.
source: Although Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs had comparable phagocytic activity to WT controls when macrophages were kept as cell suspensions during the incubation with PS-attached beads (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), these mutant BMDMs showed clearly reduced bead internalization in the 3D matrix (Figure 6B and C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mesenchymal-like migrating Itgb2−/− BMDMs did not show impaired bead sampling.
source: Impaired haptokinesis of amoeboid-shaped Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs impeded efficient space exploration and bead sampling, which was not observed for mesenchymal-like migrating Itgb2−/− BMDMs (Figure 6A–C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rudimentary movement of Itgb1−/− BMDMs was sufficient to sample beads in close vicinity to them, but the restricted movement radius prevented bead sampling of larger areas.
source: Live-cell imaging analysis revealed that the rudimentary movement of Itgb1−/− BMDMs was sufficient to sample beads in close vicinity to them, but the restricted movement radius prevented bead sampling of larger areas (Figure 6D and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—video 1.

claim: Doubling the cell number in the macrophage population rescued the surveillance deficit of Itgb1−/− BMDM networks.
source: However, we could rescue this surveillance deficit of Itgb1−/− BMDM networks by doubling the cell number in the macrophage population (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: A network of 300–400 macrophages was able to remove 500–700 dead neutrophils within 24–30 hr.
source: Efferocytosis was extremely efficient and a network of 300–400 macrophages was able to remove 500–700 dead neutrophils within 24–30 hr (Figure 7B and Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—video 1.

claim: Individual WT BMDMs sequentially ingested 8–14 cells over 24–30 hr.
source: Microscopic observation of individual WT BMDMs revealed a spectrum of mesenchymal-like movement behaviors that supported efficient efferocytosis, including individual macrophages that sequentially ingested 8–14 cells over 24–30 hr (Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and ).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Networks of Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs were significantly impaired in the removal of dead neutrophils.
source: Testing the efferocytic capacity of integrin-deficient BMDM networks, we made again the striking observation that β1 integrin-dependent haptokinesis was crucial for optimal surveillance. As observed for the sampling of PS-attached beads that do not release 'find-me' signals, networks of Tln1−/− and Itgb1−/− BMDMs were significantly impaired in the removal of dead neutrophils.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The phenotype of Tln1−/− BMDMs was even more pronounced in comparison to Itgb1−/− BMDMs, probably due to migration-independent effects of talin on αv integrins.
source: The phenotype of Tln1−/− BMDMs was even more pronounced in comparison to Itgb1−/− BMDMs, probably due to migration-independent effects of talin on αv integrins, which contribute to dead cell recognition and uptake (Lemke, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and speculation based on citation to previous work.

claim: Itgb2−/− BMDMs showed similar efferocytic activities as WT cells.
source: In contrast, Itgb2−/− BMDMs showed similar efferocytic activities as WT cells (Figure 7C and D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C, D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Haptokinetic movement of mesenchymal-shaped WT BMDMs at speeds of ~0.6 µm/min supported efficient sampling of corpses and surveillance of large areas.
source: Haptokinetic movement of mesenchymal-shaped WT BMDMs at speeds of ~0.6 µm/min supported efficient sampling of corpses and surveillance of large areas (Figure 7E and ), whereas impaired haptokinesis of Itgb1−/− BMDMs restricted surveillance to smaller regions (Figure 7F and Figure 7—video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Impaired haptokinesis of Itgb1−/− BMDMs restricted surveillance to smaller regions.
source: Haptokinetic movement of mesenchymal-shaped WT BMDMs at speeds of ~0.6 µm/min supported efficient sampling of corpses and surveillance of large areas (Figure 7E and ), whereas impaired haptokinesis of Itgb1−/− BMDMs restricted surveillance to smaller regions (Figure 7F and Figure 7—video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—video 3.

claim: Individual Itgb1−/− macrophages could ingest several dead neutrophils, but the slow amoeboid-like movement limited their efferocytic sampling to only nearby corpses.
source: Although individual Itgb1−/− macrophages could ingest several dead neutrophils, the slow amoeboid-like movement limited their efferocytic sampling to only nearby corpses (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cortical macrophages sit on an ECM-rich reticular fiber scaffold, where they form dense cellular networks.
source: These cortical macrophages sit on an ECM-rich reticular fiber scaffold, where they form dense cellular networks (Bellomo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cortical macrophages act as the only professional phagocyte that continuously clears apoptotic cells in the T cell zone of lymph nodes.
source: Previous work has shown that this tissue-resident macrophage type acts as the only professional phagocyte that continuously clears apoptotic cells in the T cell zone of lymph nodes (Baratin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cortical macrophages in lymph nodes of WT mice showed elongated protrusions and multi-branched, mesenchymal-like shapes.
source: Confocal immunofluorescence analysis revealed dense networks of cortical macrophages with elongated protrusions and multi-branched, mesenchymal-like shapes in the T cell zones of WT mice (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Cortical macrophages in lymph nodes of conditional Itgb1 knockout mice were more roundish and showed amoeboid-like morphologies.
source: In contrast, cortical macrophages in lymph nodes of conditional Itgb1 knockout mice were more roundish and showed amoeboid-like morphologies (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Mice with Itgb1-deficient macrophages showed a significantly increased number of extracellular, non-internalized apoptotic cells in T cell zones in comparison to littermate control mice.
source: Importantly, mice with Itgb1-deficient macrophages showed a significantly increased number of extracellular, non-internalized apoptotic cells in T cell zones in comparison to littermate control mice (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Hemocytes utilize two distinct modes of engulfment, 'lamellipodial' and 'filopodial' phagocytosis, which provide individual cells phagocytic plasticity to fulfill their clearance functions.
source: Recent work in Drosophila embryos have strengthened this view by showing that hemocytes utilize two distinct modes of engulfment, 'lamellipodial' and 'filopodial' phagocytosis, which provide individual cells phagocytic plasticity to fulfill their clearance functions (Davidson and Wood, 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The efficiency of detecting, engulfing, and clearing dead cell corpses depends on the efferocytic capacity of a whole macrophage population.
source: This population behavior is important for the removal of dead cell material in tissues, where the efficiency of detecting, engulfing, and clearing dead cell corpses depends on the efferocytic capacity of a whole macrophage population, which sometimes even requires additional support from non-professional phagocytes (Damisah et al., 2020; Han et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Molecules recognizing 'find-me' and 'eat-me' signals and their surface expression levels on individual cells are important determinants for the efferocytic capacity of macrophage populations.
source: Hence, it is evident that molecules recognizing 'find-me' and 'eat-me' signals and their surface expression levels on individual cells are important determinants for the efferocytic capacity of macrophage populations (Hughes et al., 2021; Rothlin and Ghosh, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both surveillance modes (surveillance by migration and surveillance by low-motile protrusion extension) are likely reflected in the heterogeneity of resident macrophages in mammalian tissues.
source: We speculate that both surveillance modes are likely reflected in the heterogeneity of resident macrophages in mammalian tissues (Blériot et al., 2020; Cox et al., 2021), contributing to the robustness of macrophage network function.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings and citations to previous work on macrophage heterogeneity.

claim: Integrin β1-mediated substrate binding controls the 3D mesenchymal-like shape, movement, lamellopodial protrusiveness, and space exploration of individual cells in a sampling macrophage network.
source: As the most important result of our study, we identify that both surveillance strategies critically depend on haptokinesis. Integrin β1-mediated substrate binding controls the 3D mesenchymal-like shape, movement, lamellopodial protrusiveness, and space exploration of individual cells in a sampling macrophage network.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Loss of β1 integrin function switches the cells to an amoeboid-like morphology, which does not support random motility and the sampling of particles or dead cells by the macrophage network.
source: Loss of β1 integrin function switches the cells to an amoeboid-like morphology, which does not support random motility and the sampling of particles or dead cells by the macrophage network.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Randomly migrating mouse macrophages cannot compensate for the loss of integrin function and the associated switch from a mesenchymal- to an amoeboid-like morphology.
source: In contrast to many other immune cell types (Lämmermann and Germain, 2014), we find that randomly migrating mouse macrophages cannot compensate for the loss of integrin function and the associated switch from a mesenchymal- to an amoeboid-like morphology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous studies on other immune cells.

claim: Studies with hMDMs invading 3D collagen gels found classical focal adhesion and podosome components at the tip of F-actin-rich cell protrusions together with β1 integrins.
source: Interestingly, studies with hMDMs invading 3D collagen gels found classical focal adhesion and podosome components (e.g. talin, paxillin, vinculin) at the tip of F-actin-rich cell protrusions together with β1 integrins (Van Goethem et al., 2011; Wiesner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When talin- or β1 integrin-deficient macrophages were exposed to gradients of high C5a attractant concentrations, these amoeboid-shaped cells polarized their leading edges toward the attractant source and moved chemotactically with speeds similar to control cells.
source: To our surprise, we find contrasting integrin demands of random and chemotactic macrophage migration. When talin- or β1 integrin-deficient macrophages were exposed to gradients of high C5a attractant concentrations, these amoeboid-shaped cells polarized their leading edges toward the attractant source and moved chemotactically with speeds similar to control cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Strong chemotactic signals can induce and maintain the polarization of the macrophage actomyosin cytoskeleton, enabling productive migration in the absence of integrin-dependent substrate binding.
source: Thus, strong chemotactic signals can induce and maintain the polarization of the macrophage actomyosin cytoskeleton, enabling productive migration in the absence of integrin-dependent substrate binding.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing integrin-independent chemotaxis.

claim: Randomly migrating macrophages lost their mesenchymal phenotype upon CK-666 treatment and were impaired in their speed and displacement.
source: Similar to integrins, we find contrasting demands of Arp2/3 activity for random versus chemotactic 3D migration. Randomly migrating macrophages lost their mesenchymal phenotype upon CK-666 treatment and were impaired in their speed and displacement.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Movement of CK-666-treated macrophages along a strong chemotactic gradient was unimpaired.
source: Yet, movement of CK-666-treated macrophages along a strong chemotactic gradient was unimpaired, which is in agreement with several previous studies on fibroblasts (Asokan et al., 2014; Dimchev et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2012), BMDMs (Rotty et al., 2017), and other immune cell types (Georgantzoglou et al., 2021; Leithner et al., 2016; Moreau et al., 2015; Vargas et al., 2016), supporting the general notion that dendritic actin networks rather inhibit than support persistent movement along chemotactic cues and in confined environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Macrophages strictly depend on integrin-mediated ECM interactions to establish lamellopodial protrusions as exploratory structures.
source: As seen for low-adhesive neutrophils and dendritic cells (Georgantzoglou et al., 2021; Leithner et al., 2016), macrophages also rely on Arp2/3-mediated front actin networks for space exploration in complex environments. However, macrophages strictly depend on integrin-mediated ECM interactions to establish lamellopodial protrusions as exploratory structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Individual dying cells release only low amounts of attractants, which generate chemotactic signals that are too weak and transient to support the full polarization of the macrophage cytoskeleton in the absence of functional integrins.
source: Although we showed that integrin receptors were dispensable for 3D macrophage chemotaxis, integrin-mediated movement and protrusiveness was absolutely critical for efferocytosis by a surveying macrophage network. We speculate that individual dying cells release only low amounts of attractants, which generate chemotactic signals that are too weak and transient to support the full polarization of the macrophage cytoskeleton in the absence of functional integrins.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings.

claim: Integrin-dependent stabilization of the mesenchymal-like cell shape is crucial for efficient efferocytosis by macrophage networks.
source: Thus, integrin-dependent stabilization of the mesenchymal-like cell shape is crucial for efficient efferocytosis by macrophage networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing impaired efferocytosis in integrin-deficient macrophages.

claim: β2 integrins appear not to be involved in pro-migratory mechanotransduction in interstitial environments.
source: β2 integrins, which are abundantly expressed on macrophages, appear not to be involved in pro-migratory mechanotransduction in these interstitial environments, and likely serve other macrophage functions (e.g. pattern recognition, complement- and IgG-mediated phagocytosis, cell retention) (Cui et al., 2018; Jaumouillé et al., 2019; Torres-Gomez et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: αV integrins may rather support other macrophage functions such as apoptotic cell uptake and TGFβ activation.
source: αV integrins, which we did not target in this study, may also rather support other macrophage functions (e.g. apoptotic cell uptake, TGFβ activation) (Kelly et al., 2018; Lemke, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on citations to previous work.

claim: For organs and tissue compartments with largely cellular composition, the maintenance of the mesenchymal-like macrophage phenotype may not necessarily require integrin-dependent ECM binding.
source: For organs and tissue compartments with largely cellular composition (e.g. brain, glands, epithelial layers), the maintenance of the mesenchymal-like macrophage phenotype may not necessarily require integrin-dependent ECM binding (Brand et al., 2020; Meller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on citations to previous work.

claim: Substrate-dependent movement and protrusiveness are critical determinants for space exploration and efficient sampling of macrophage networks.
source: In summary, our study highlights macrophages as a tissue-resident immune cell type that does not follow the general prevailing paradigm of integrin-independent 3D migration of immune cells. Substrate-dependent movement and protrusiveness are critical determinants for space exploration and efficient sampling of macrophage networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Integrins are not only critical for the migratory processes of intravascular crawling, extravasation, and invasion, but also crucial for the interstitial movement of myeloid immune cell subsets.
source: Thus, integrins are not only critical for the migratory processes of intravascular crawling (Neupane et al., 2020), extravasation (Nourshargh et al., 2010), and invasion (Arasa et al., 2021), but also crucial for the interstitial movement of myeloid immune cell subsets.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and citations to previous work.
